After a little heat, regarding the silver, provided it is also informed with the form of silver, it can result in gold more easily than from other metals, unless it is deprived of its heat, or its natural operation is taken away from it. But if the virtue of a greater natural heat reaches this quicksilver before it is formed to its end, namely into the form of silver, so that it is reduced into the pure and red sulfur of nature, then gold is made from it more quickly than silver, and it remains in it perpetually, as the end will be toward which nature strives by laboring.

Quicksilver, which we have just mentioned, is the mother of all metals because of its coldness and humidity. And if it becomes pure and separated from every superfluity, then no further coarseness can be mixed with it, such that it might be reduced again into some imperfect metal. For nature does not work backward, nor is there any matter that looks toward some impure form, such as imperfect metals are. But sulfur is the father of all metals because of its heat and dryness. According to this difference, let it be observed that quicksilver is described in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER II.

There is, therefore, in all metals a true Mercury and a proper sulfur, equally in imperfect as well as in perfect metals. It has merely become contaminated and impure in imperfect metals, which are deprived only of perfect maturation. And for the same reasons, they can be reduced to gold and silver, that is, so that the impurity with which they had been polluted may be separated from the golden or silver nature that is in them, and the form of gold or silver may be instilled into them. For they have been torn away from nature because they were removed and excavated from natural passages, mines, and veins of the earth. Therefore, they can no longer have any operation in themselves as if they were still lying hidden under the earth; nevertheless, as much as lies within them, they desire to be perfected.
